blindSummary: Research located no state/province-specific statute, enforcement series, or event finding for this unit; the sources describe only the national framework, which applies here in full.
blindSourceSummaries: NOTE: page content did not load at fetch time (a foreign news outlet returned an access-denied security page); the underlying July 2026 live-news report covers a national court sending a person convicted of neo-Nazi incitement - whose legal gender had been changed under the country's gender-recognition law - to a men's prison amid public outcry over women's-prison safety, the case that drove the state-level prison-placement law debate discussed in the accompanying analyses.

A constitutional-law blog essay (18 March 2026): in the wake of the neo-Nazi prison-placement controversy, it documents that most states/provinces quietly reformed their prison-placement statutes from 2023 on (one new prison-execution act in force 1 March 2026, with three more states/provinces having analogous rules), analyses that placement rules tied to the civil-status gender entry must respect the national gender-recognition law's rule that the current entry governs, and defends inclusive exceptions - e.g. placing a trans woman per her self-expressed gender even before correcting her entry - as constitutional, citing the national constitutional court's 1996 self-identification case law.

A foreign public broadcaster feature (23 August 2023): how the country's prisons deal with trans inmates - a transgender climate activist (legal sex 'male') facing possible men's-prison placement illustrates the structural problem; the prison-staff union's federal chair says men's prisons are inadequately prepared and understaffed (~2,000 officer shortage among ~60,000 detainees) to protect trans prisoners; prison administration is a state/province competence (16 states/provinces nationwide), several with special arrangements; civil-society estimates put the trans population at up to 500,000.
